summary: Specifies a SIP private header, P-Refused-URI-List, used in the Open Mobile Alliance's Push to talk over Cellular system. It lets URI-list servers refuse to handle incoming URI lists that contain embedded lists, and tell the client about the embedded lists they refused. It is informational and has since been updated.

plainLanguage.summary: Pretend you ask a mail room to send a message to a list of people, and one name on it is another list. This is how the mail room says no thanks and which one it refused.

subtitle: A SIP header that lets a server refuse a request containing nested URI lists and hand back the members instead.

tldr.problem: In Push to talk over Cellular, the server that sets up an ad-hoc group session may receive a URI list whose entries are themselves lists. The server holding such a list cannot invite its members, because it is not the controlling server for the session, and SIP had no way to say so.
tldr.mechanism: The server answers with a 403 (Forbidden) response carrying one or more P-Refused-URI-List header fields. Each names a refused list URI and may point, by Content-ID, to a body part holding that list's members.
tldr.outcome: The client can then send requests directly to the members. The RFC says the header has no general applicability outside OMA PoC. It was later updated by RFC 8217.

facts.label: Context
facts.value: OMA Push to talk over Cellular

today: RFC 5318 is an Informational RFC and was updated by RFC 8217. The text itself says the header does not seem to have general applicability outside OMA PoC.

sections.title: The Ad-Hoc Group Problem
sections.content:
The Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) defined Push to talk over Cellular (PoC), which uses SIP and URI-list services. An ad-hoc PoC group session is one where the originator picks participants on the fly, for example from an address book, and sends an INVITE with a URI list. The PoC network sends an individual INVITE to each URI.

Later versions of the service let the originator include entries that are themselves URI lists, such as a pre-arranged PoC group. The members of those embedded lists should be invited too.

An ad-hoc session always has exactly one controlling PoC server, which resolves the list and acts as the focus of the session. Each participant has a participating PoC server in their home domain. The server for a pre-arranged group knows its members but cannot send INVITEs itself, since it is not the controlling server. It needs a way to tell the controlling server who the members are, and SIP had none. This document defines that mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: One person in charge sends out invitations. If one name on the guest list is a whole club, the club's secretary cannot send invitations. The secretary has to tell the person in charge who is in the club.

sections.title: How the Refusal Works
sections.content:
When a URI-list server receives an INVITE whose URI list contains entries that are lists, and it cannot handle the request, it returns a 403 (Forbidden) response with a P-Refused-URI-List P-Header. The header holds the members of the list or lists that caused the rejection, so the client can send requests directly to those members.

A 403 response can contain more than one P-Refused-URI-List entry. The header MUST NOT be used with any other response. Each entry carries a URI that was in the incoming list and could not be handled, and can optionally carry some or all of that list's members.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is a polite no, with a note attached saying which list was the problem and who is on it.

sections.title: Header Syntax and Body Parts
sections.content:
The header is a comma-separated list of entries. Each entry is a name-addr or addr-spec, optionally followed by semicolon-separated parameters. The defined parameter is members, whose value MUST be a cid-url as defined in RFC 2392. Unknown parameters fall under generic-param.

The 403 response MAY carry body parts that contain URI lists. An entry refers to a body part through its Content-ID, and if a Content-ID is given, one body part MUST have an equivalent Content-ID. The format of a URI list is service specific. This lets the client tell which URI relates to which list, if the server is willing to disclose that.
sections.plainLanguage: Each refused list gets a label, and the label points to a page in the attachments that shows who is on it.

sections.title: A Worked Exchange
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, a controlling PoC server at example.com sends an INVITE to the participating PoC server at example.net. The body carries an XML resource list with three entries: sip:bob@example.net, sip:friends-list@example.net and sip:colleagues-list@example.net. The last two are pre-arranged groups.

The participating server replies with 403 Forbidden and two P-Refused-URI-List fields, one per list, each with a members parameter pointing at a Content-ID. A multipart body holds one resource list per Content-ID. The controlling server can then see the members that the participating server chose to disclose, and can deduce that the participating server sent no outgoing requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The controlling server asks about three names. Two are clubs. The reply says no to the two clubs and attaches a sheet for each club listing its members.

sections.title: Applicability and Security
sections.content:
The header is intended for OMA PoC networks and is used between PoC servers. In a PoC session only one server can resolve incoming URI lists, a restriction that services on the public Internet do not have. The header also needs trust relationships between servers that do not typically exist on the public Internet, so the RFC says it does not seem to have general applicability outside OMA PoC. It is optional and only gives clients extra information about the refusal.

The elements are assumed trusted and in the operators' core network, with traffic protection by IPsec and sometimes physical protection. Two risks are named. Eavesdropping: 403 responses may reveal list members, so hop-by-hop or end-to-end encryption (TLS or S/MIME) is RECOMMENDED. Disclosing information: a server should reveal list contents only to authorized clients, which is RECOMMENDED.

IANA added the header field and the members parameter to the SIP Parameters registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The note names the people in a club, so only trusted people should be able to read it, and the reply should be kept in a sealed envelope.
